title: Erythrocytosis Workup: PV, Secondary and Relative
summary: Learn how to confirm a high hemoglobin, separate apparent from true erythrocytosis, use JAK2, marrow and EPO to distinguish polycythemia vera from secondary causes, and find a high-oxygen-affinity hemoglobin that routine HPLC can miss.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 33 Hit 12 (PV: low EPO + JAK2 vs secondary high/appropriate EPO), Hit 17 (relative erythrocytosis) and Exam Trap 4 (normal electrophoresis does not exclude a high-affinity hemoglobin). Checked against Gangat 2021, Barbui 2018 (2016 WHO criteria table read via a page-fetch tool), Khoury 2022 (WHO 5th edition), Mori 2023, Souresho 2021 and the BSH 2019 guideline (McMullin 2019). Hit 12 is qualified (register flag rv-ch33-epo-not-specific): a subnormal EPO is only a WHO minor criterion, hypoxic secondary erythrocytosis often has a normal EPO, and about 40% of non-neoplastic erythrocytosis in Mori 2023 had a low EPO. Trap 4 is extended (register flag rv-ch33-high-affinity-hb-sequencing): HPLC is normal in about one-third of high-affinity variants, so globin sequencing is often needed; the reviewer’s “arterial O₂ saturation” step was not found in the sources read and is not taught. Hit 17’s “rehydrate … not phlebotomy” is not taught as a rule: the sources read define relative erythrocytosis as reduced plasma volume and require confirmation on repeat counts but do not state a rehydration protocol. The StatPearls “Secondary Polycythemia” chapter (NCBI Bookshelf) was blocked by a captcha and was not read.

objectives: Apply the 2016 WHO hemoglobin/hematocrit thresholds and confirm erythrocytosis on repeat counts.
Distinguish true from apparent (relative) erythrocytosis, and polycythemia vera from secondary erythrocytosis using JAK2, marrow and EPO.
Explain why a normal hemoglobin HPLC does not exclude a high-oxygen-affinity variant and what p50 shows.

scenes.title: Three high hemoglobins
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three adults with a high hemoglobin. (1) A 62-year-old man, Hb 18.4 g/dL, JAK2 V617F detected, serum EPO below the reference range. (2) A 48-year-old woman on a diuretic after a bout of vomiting, Hct 50% on one count, JAK2 negative, EPO normal. (3) A 24-year-old man with a high Hb on every count since his teens and a brother with the same, JAK2 negative, EPO normal, hemoglobin HPLC normal. Question token: “Clonal, called-for, or concentrated?”

cues.text: Three adults arrive with a high hemoglobin. The first is sixty-two, with a JAK2 mutation and a low erythropoietin.
The second is on a diuretic after vomiting, with one high hematocrit. The third has been high since his teens, like his brother, and his hemoglobin HPLC is normal.
Which of these is a marrow disease, which is a response, and which is not extra red cells at all?

scenes.title: Is it real?
scenes.altText: Two cards. Threshold card: the 2016 WHO polycythemia vera criteria use hemoglobin above 16.5 g/dL in men or 16.0 g/dL in women, or hematocrit above 49% in men or 48% in women; erythrocytosis should be confirmed on at least two counts taken at different times. Split card: true (absolute) erythrocytosis = more red cells, either clonal (polycythemia vera) or non-clonal (secondary); apparent erythrocytosis = reduced plasma volume (relative erythrocytosis) or an extreme normal value above the 95th percentile.

cues.text: First, is the number really high? The 2016 WHO criteria for polycythemia vera use a hemoglobin above sixteen point five in men or sixteen in women, or a hematocrit above forty-nine or forty-eight percent.
One count is not enough. Erythrocytosis should be confirmed on at least two counts taken at different times.
True erythrocytosis means more red cells: either a clonal marrow disease, polycythemia vera, or a non-clonal, secondary process.
Apparent erythrocytosis is not extra red cells. Usually the plasma volume has shrunk, a relative erythrocytosis; sometimes it is simply an extreme normal value.

scenes.title: JAK2 and EPO split the true cases
scenes.altText: Two cards. Polycythemia vera card (WHO 2016): major criteria — Hb/Hct above threshold (or increased red cell mass), marrow hypercellular with trilineage growth (panmyelosis), JAK2 V617F or JAK2 exon 12 mutation; minor criterion — subnormal serum EPO; diagnosis = all three major, or the first two major plus the minor. JAK2 V617F is found in about 95% of PV. Secondary card: EPO normal or high; hypoxic causes (COPD, cyanotic heart disease, high altitude) often have a normal, compensated EPO; EPO-producing tumors; drugs such as testosterone and erythropoiesis-stimulating agents. Caveat token: a low EPO is not proof of PV — about 40% of JAK2-negative non-neoplastic erythrocytosis in one cohort had EPO below normal, and EPOR mutations give a subnormal EPO.

cues.text: For polycythemia vera, the WHO major criteria are the high hemoglobin or hematocrit, a hypercellular marrow with growth of all three lines, and a JAK2 V617F or exon 12 mutation. V617F is found in about ninety-five percent.
A subnormal erythropoietin is only a minor criterion. The diagnosis needs all three major criteria, or the first two plus the low erythropoietin.

Secondary erythrocytosis is driven by erythropoietin, which is normal or high. In hypoxia from lung disease, cyanotic heart disease or altitude, it is often normal because it is compensated. Tumors that make erythropoietin, testosterone and stimulating drugs are other causes.
So a low erythropoietin is not proof of polycythemia vera. In one cohort, about forty percent of non-clonal cases had a value below normal, and receptor mutations give a low value too.

scenes.title: When the hemoglobin holds on too tight
scenes.altText: Schematic oxygen dissociation curves: a normal curve and a left-shifted curve with a lower p50. Card: high-oxygen-affinity hemoglobin variants release less oxygen to tissue, the kidney senses hypoxia, EPO rises or stays normal, and erythrocytosis follows. Venous p50 below 24 mmHg = left shift (high-affinity Hb, 2,3-BPG deficiency, or methemoglobinemia). Variants are detected by cation-exchange HPLC, capillary electrophoresis or mass spectrometry, but HPLC is normal in about one-third, so HBB, HBA1 and HBA2 sequencing is often needed. Hook answers: (1) clonal — polycythemia vera workup; (2) concentrated — repeat the count, think plasma volume; (3) called-for — measure p50 and consider globin gene sequencing.

cues.text: Some hemoglobin variants hold oxygen too tightly. Tissue gets less oxygen, the kidney keeps erythropoietin normal or high, and red cells rise.

The clue is the p50, the oxygen tension at half saturation. A venous p50 below twenty-four millimeters of mercury means a left shift: a high-affinity hemoglobin, 2,3-BPG deficiency, or methemoglobinemia.
HPLC, capillary electrophoresis or mass spectrometry can find the variant, but HPLC is normal in about a third, so globin gene sequencing is often needed.
Back to the hook: the first patient is clonal. The second needs a repeat count with plasma volume in mind. The third needs a p50 and, if shifted, sequencing.

props.label: HPLC normal in ~1/3 → sequence HBB, HBA1, HBA2

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Low EPO means polycythemia vera” (✓ subnormal EPO is a minor criterion; JAK2 and marrow carry the diagnosis, and some non-clonal cases have a low EPO); “Normal hemoglobin electrophoresis rules out a hemoglobinopathy” (✓ HPLC misses about a third of high-affinity variants; check p50 and sequence); “One high hematocrit is erythrocytosis” (✓ confirm on two counts at different times; low plasma volume can mimic it).

cues.text: Trap one: a low erythropoietin means polycythemia vera. No: it is only a minor criterion, and some non-clonal cases have it too.
Trap two: a normal hemoglobin study rules out a hemoglobinopathy. No: HPLC misses about a third of high-affinity variants. Check the p50 and sequence.
Trap three: one high hematocrit is erythrocytosis. No: confirm it on repeat counts, because a shrunken plasma volume can mimic it.

props.title: ✗ “Low EPO = PV.”
lines: ✓ Minor criterion only; JAK2 + marrow decide

props.title: ✗ “One high Hct = erythrocytosis.”
lines: ✓ Repeat it; low plasma volume mimics

scenes.title: Clonal, called-for, concentrated
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Three Cs of a high hemoglobin: CLONAL (polycythemia vera: JAK2, marrow, EPO usually low), CALLED-FOR (secondary: EPO normal or high, from hypoxia, tumors, drugs or a tight-binding hemoglobin), CONCENTRATED (relative: the plasma shrank, the red cells did not grow).” Tokens for each C. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: three Cs of a high hemoglobin. Clonal is polycythemia vera. Called-for is secondary, with erythropoietin normal or high. Concentrated is relative: the plasma shrank, the red cells did not grow.
Where it breaks: erythropoietin overlaps between the groups, many true cases stay unexplained even after full testing, and a normal hemoglobin study does not exclude a tight-binding variant.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Confirm on repeat counts · true or apparent?”, “JAK2 + marrow for PV · low EPO is minor · normal HPLC can miss high-affinity Hb”.

cues.text: Confirm a high hemoglobin on repeat counts, diagnose polycythemia vera with JAK2 and the marrow rather than a low erythropoietin alone, and check the p50 when a lifelong erythrocytosis has a normal hemoglobin study.

props.label: Repeat the count · true or apparent?
PV = JAK2 + marrow · low EPO minor · normal HPLC → p50

explanation.what: Plain language: a high hemoglobin can mean the marrow is overproducing on its own, the body is asking for more red cells, or the blood is simply concentrated because plasma is low. Scientific terms: absolute (true) and apparent erythrocytosis, relative erythrocytosis (reduced plasma volume), polycythemia vera (PV), JAK2 V617F and exon 12 mutations, panmyelosis, serum erythropoietin (EPO), secondary erythrocytosis, high-oxygen-affinity hemoglobin, p50, 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG).
explanation.why: PV is a clonal myeloproliferative neoplasm driven by JAK2 mutations, so EPO is usually suppressed. Secondary erythrocytosis is EPO-driven: hypoxia, EPO-producing tumors, drugs, or a hemoglobin that releases oxygen poorly (left-shifted curve). Relative erythrocytosis raises the concentration of red cells without increasing their number.
explanation.measure: WHO 2016 PV: Hb > 16.5 g/dL (men) / > 16.0 g/dL (women) or Hct > 49% / > 48%; major criteria Hb/Hct, marrow panmyelosis, JAK2 V617F or exon 12; minor criterion subnormal EPO; all three major or first two plus minor. Confirm erythrocytosis on at least two counts at different times. Venous p50 < 24 mmHg = left shift. High-affinity variants: HPLC, capillary electrophoresis or mass spectrometry, but HPLC normal in about one-third, so HBB/HBA1/HBA2 sequencing is often needed.
explanation.differs: PV (JAK2 +, EPO usually subnormal, panmyelosis) vs secondary (JAK2 −, EPO normal or high) vs relative (reduced plasma volume, not more red cells). Low EPO is not exclusive to PV: EPOR mutations and some non-neoplastic erythrocytosis also show it.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: classify a high-Hb case from JAK2 and EPO, recognise that a low EPO is a minor criterion only, pick p50/sequencing after a normal hemoglobin study in familial erythrocytosis, or choose to repeat the count in suspected plasma-volume loss.

comparisons.title: Polycythemia vera vs secondary erythrocytosis
comparisons.distinguisher: Clonal JAK2-driven marrow vs EPO-driven response.

comparisons.title: True vs apparent erythrocytosis
comparisons.distinguisher: Whether red cells are increased or only concentrated.

mnemonic.text: Three Cs of a high hemoglobin: CLONAL (polycythemia vera), CALLED-FOR (secondary, EPO normal or high), CONCENTRATED (relative: the plasma shrank, the red cells did not grow).
mnemonic.explanation: Sorts erythrocytosis by mechanism: marrow clone, EPO-driven response, or plasma loss.
mnemonic.limitation: EPO overlaps between groups (some non-clonal cases have a low EPO; hypoxic cases often have a normal one); many true cases remain unexplained after full testing; a normal hemoglobin HPLC can miss a high-affinity variant.

analogyLimitations: The three Cs leave out idiopathic erythrocytosis, which is common.
takeaway: Confirm a high hemoglobin on repeat counts, diagnose polycythemia vera with JAK2 and the marrow rather than a low erythropoietin alone, and check the p50 when a lifelong erythrocytosis has a normal hemoglobin study.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man has had Hb 18–19 g/dL on every count since adolescence; his brother is similar. JAK2 V617F and exon 12 are negative, EPO is normal, and hemoglobin HPLC is normal. What is the best next step?

options.text: Measure venous p50 and, if left-shifted, sequence the globin genes
options.rationale: Correct. HPLC is normal in about one-third of high-affinity variants; a low p50 and HBB/HBA1/HBA2 sequencing find them.

options.text: Conclude that a hemoglobinopathy has been excluded
options.rationale: Incorrect. A normal HPLC does not exclude a high-oxygen-affinity variant.
Incorrect. JAK2 is negative and EPO is not subnormal; lifelong familial erythrocytosis points to a hereditary cause.
Incorrect. A sustained, lifelong, familial elevation is not explained by a transient fall in plasma volume.

questions.stem: Which finding is a MINOR rather than a major criterion for polycythemia vera in the 2016 WHO classification?

options.rationale: Correct. A subnormal EPO is the single minor criterion.

options.text: JAK2 V617F or JAK2 exon 12 mutation
options.rationale: Incorrect. The JAK2 mutation is a major criterion.
Incorrect. Marrow morphology is a major criterion.

options.text: Hemoglobin above 16.5 g/dL in a man
options.rationale: Incorrect. The hemoglobin/hematocrit threshold is a major criterion.

questions.stem: A woman on a diuretic, recovering from several days of vomiting, has a single hematocrit of 50%. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: Erythrocytosis must be confirmed on repeat counts, and a reduced plasma volume can raise the hematocrit without more red cells
options.rationale: Correct. Relative erythrocytosis reflects low plasma volume, and erythrocytosis should be confirmed on at least two counts at different times.

options.text: A hematocrit above 48% in a woman establishes polycythemia vera
options.rationale: Incorrect. The threshold is only one major criterion; PV also needs marrow findings and JAK2 or the minor EPO criterion.

options.text: A normal EPO here proves secondary erythrocytosis from hypoxia
options.rationale: Incorrect. A normal EPO does not show that the red cell mass is increased; a true erythrocytosis has not been established.

options.text: A low EPO, if found, would confirm polycythemia vera
options.rationale: Incorrect. A subnormal EPO is only a minor criterion and occurs in some non-neoplastic erythrocytosis.

claims.text: WHO 2016 Hb/Hct thresholds; confirm on at least two counts at different times.
True vs apparent erythrocytosis; relative erythrocytosis = reduced plasma volume.
WHO PV major/minor criteria and combination rule; JAK2 V617F in about 95%.
Secondary erythrocytosis: EPO normal or high; hypoxic causes often normal EPO; tumors and drugs.
Low EPO is not specific for PV (about 40% of non-neoplastic cases in one cohort; EPOR mutations; a third of idiopathic).
High-affinity Hb mechanism; venous p50 < 24 mmHg causes; HPLC normal in one-third; globin sequencing.
Rehydrate rather than phlebotomise in relative erythrocytosis; arterial O₂ saturation as a check for high-affinity hemoglobin.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 33 Hit 12 pairs PV with low EPO and secondary erythrocytosis with high/appropriate EPO. A subnormal EPO is only a WHO minor criterion (Barbui 2018); hypoxic secondary erythrocytosis often has a normal EPO (Gangat 2021); about 40% of JAK2-negative non-neoplastic erythrocytosis had EPO below normal (Mori 2023), and EPOR mutations cause a subnormal EPO (register flag rv-ch33-epo-not-specific).

Ch. 33 Exam Trap 4 advises p50 and arterial O₂ saturation after a normal electrophoresis. Gangat 2021 adds that HPLC is normal in about one-third of high-affinity variants so HBB/HBA1/HBA2 sequencing is often needed, and that a low p50 also occurs with 2,3-BPG deficiency and methemoglobinemia; the arterial-saturation step was not found in the sources read (register flag rv-ch33-high-affinity-hb-sequencing).
